item.title: Sorting 'Good' Single-Homeowners from 'Bad' Ones: Avoiding Self-Defeating Moves (‘착한 1주택자’와 ‘나쁜 1주택자’ 가르기, 자충수 안 되려면)
item.description:
<<>> Seoul is a multi-layered city. For some, it is a place of residence. One home is enough for them. For others, Seoul is a place of migration in pursuit of opportunity. With universities and jobs concentrated here, entering the city is crucial. Ownership is not a must—whether jeonse (lump-sum deposit rental) or monthly rent, once inside, one gains access to the network of opportunities. For yet others, Seoul is a place of ownership. Over the past 15 years, few assets have guaranteed returns as stable and high as Seoul's premier apartment complexes. These three demands from different strata collide in the single space of Seoul. A solution that satisfies all of them simultaneously is hard to find. This is the challenge now facing the Lee Jae-myung administration. <<> Since the launch of the Lee Jae-myung administration, Korea's real estate problem has effectively been equated with Seoul—more precisely, with Seoul apartments. The shock that followed August's tax reform proposal was likewise concentrated in Seoul. In areas dense with ultra-high-end apartments such as Gangnam and Seocho, listings have increased and prices have fallen—a welcome signal, as it means adjustment pressure has begun to work on high-priced homes. But this change alone should not lead us to underestimate the policy's side effects. Outside Gangnam and Seocho, upward movements are being observed across Seoul generally and in some high-priced apartment areas in Gyeonggi Province. If prices in ultra-high-end areas fall somewhat while housing values fluctuate across a wider region, that is not stability but a transfer of instability. The success of the policy should be judged not by price declines in a few Gangnam apartment complexes, but by how stable prices and transaction volumes remain across Seoul and the broader capital region. A situation where instability spreads beyond ultra-high-end areas into mid- and low-priced neighborhoods is something to guard against even more. ()

When Falling Listings in Gangnam Become the Policy Challenge <<> The first thing to assess now is whether this shockwave will spread beyond Seoul to the capital region and nationwide. On this matter, my reference point is the chase-buying—'panic buying'—observed nationwide in 2020. While researching the Seoul apartment market during the Moon Jae-in administration, I used the share of purchases by buyers in their 30s and the share of gifts (transfers) in Gangnam as key indicators. Now, the movements of both indicators are unsettling. Buyers in their 30s have returned to the forefront of purchasing, and the share of gifts in Gangnam District has roughly doubled while the Seoul average has remained flat. <<> Why do these indicators matter? Because both are tied to market participants' future expectations. Under current conditions, a person in their 30s buying a Seoul apartment is a decision difficult to make without confidence in price appreciation. The same goes for gifting property. Even under regulatory pressure, if multi-homeowners believe future capital gains will grow larger, they choose to keep assets within the family rather than sell. Underlying such behavior is a distrust of supply—a prediction that sufficient housing will not be readily available in the parts of Seoul people want within the next few years. The recent disputes over Yongsan Park and Tancheon sites reinforce that belief. Both sites are public land, where the burden of coordinating interests—such as land expropriation or resident consent—is relatively small, yet feasibility remains uncertain even now. When central and local governments cannot even reach agreement on the fastest-developable land, the market learns one message: building new apartments in Seoul is difficult. <<> Even more disconcerting is the jeonse market. A year ago on this very page, I said that while Seoul jeonse prices were rising, transaction volumes were holding steady, so it was not yet a cause for concern. But since then, transaction volumes have clearly declined while the pace of jeonse price increases has actually accelerated. The premise of that earlier diagnosis is now crumbling, which worries me greatly. <<> The 2020 'Panic Buying' and Its Possible Return in Seoul <<> However, it is too early to conclude that Seoul's real estate market will again spiral into 2020-style panic buying. Several reasons exist. First is the interest rate level. The bull market then was a product of the anomalous 'near-zero interest rate' environment during the COVID period. In hindsight, the decisive factor that ended panic buying was not increased supply but the U.S. Federal Reserve's steep rate hikes beginning in March 2022. Of course, considering the accumulated overheating during the Moon administration, the price declines under the Yoon Suk-yeol administration are hard to regard as sufficient adjustment. Rather, that government propped up the market with deregulation and policy financing, reducing the depth and duration of the correction. As a result, previous surges and excessive expectations were left inadequately resolved. In particular, the Bank of Korea was cautious about further hikes after early 2023 citing domestic and external conditions, and while the Korea-U.S. rate gap widened, currency instability and rebounding housing prices simultaneously emerged as policy burdens. Perhaps the current market instability is the price of failing to adjust sufficiently then. Fortunately, the Bank of Korea under Governor Shin Hyun-song raised rates for two consecutive months, bringing the benchmark rate to 3%. That decision was a critical choice that will shape the direction of the real estate market, and I believe it was the right call. The effects may not appear immediately, but it will constrain borrowing capacity and cool excessive sentiment, contributing to market stability. <<> Second is scope. While the 2020 bull market was a nationwide phenomenon, current attention is focused on Seoul. Even Gyeonggi Province has not yet moved with the same intensity. Finally, there is price. The average sale price of a Seoul apartment, about 870 million won in 2020, has now risen to approximately 1.58 billion won (based on KB Real Estate data). Given strong lending regulations and the possibility of further rate hikes, it is difficult to lend weight to a scenario of short-term surges like before. That said, this holds only on the premise that policy does not create new confusion in the market. <<> But why does Seoul's apartment market unrest refuse to subside? And why should we worry about its spread? It is because the core of this tax reform—owner-occupancy-centered taxation—is shaking the market. Never before has the calculus diverged so sharply between actual residents and non-residents across all stages of ownership and disposal within the same single-homeowner category. The strong reactions are therefore unsurprising. In particular, as landlords withdraw jeonse units to meet residency requirements, supply shrinks and prices rise, pushing tenants toward the "might as well buy" mindset. The current situation, where instability in both the jeonse and sale markets grows simultaneously, recalls the path following the 2020 amendment to the tenancy law, when jeonse prices shot up and the shock transferred to the sales market. This is deeply concerning. <<> How Do We Distinguish 'Good' from 'Bad' Single-Homeowners? <<> Another problem is the confusion arising from the new political cleavage this distinction creates. As Professor Oh Ji-yun of Myongji University points out, the reform package attempts to use tax law to divide 'good single-homeowners' who actually reside in their homes from 'bad single-homeowners' who do not. Yet a substantial portion of the 'constituency supporting the comprehensive real estate tax' will not readily accept this. Ownership and residence do not always coincide. A non-resident single-homeowner may have become so due to a provincial posting, children's education, or caring for parents—or due to expectations of capital gains. Life circumstances change frequently, but housing is an asset with transaction costs too high to buy and sell at every turn. Pushing these people outside the coalition overnight under the frame of 'bad single-homeowners' narrows the base sustaining the reform. The reform goals of asset-value-based taxation and curbing the 'one premium home' strategy have been obscured by the crude criterion of actual residency. Given the current unstable market conditions, it is hard to be persuaded why requiring a single-homeowner to actually reside in the home should be the top priority of real estate policy at this stage. <<> The top priority of real estate policy now should not be identifying and punishing speculators, but market stability. Nor should one declare success merely because Gangnam prices fell. If housing purchase demand spills beyond Gangnam and destabilizes prices elsewhere, the market-stabilizing effect is correspondingly offset. We must endure the gap until the effects of rate hikes materialize and supply becomes a reality. To do so, rather than adding new norms and exceptions, we should first reduce the 'noise' that undermines consistency. <<> First, we must reduce the shock created by owner-occupancy-centered taxation. The segments where tax burdens swing sharply based on residence should be smoothed out, and the incentive for landlords to withdraw jeonse units should be lowered. Contradictions between policies must also be cleaned up. Suppressing the market with strong regulation on one hand while doubling the household debt growth target on the other creates market instability. Supply is years away, but expectations of looser money are reflected in housing prices the very next day. Funds outside banking-sector regulations are no exception either. Samsung Electronics launches low-interest in-house housing loans for employees without homes starting in September. Though the intensity is controlled via area and collateral requirements, a new funding channel outside DSR has indeed been opened. In a market with thin trading, even a few high-priced transactions can move market prices, and those prices can in turn stimulate expectations across the entire market. <<> Three Divergent Views of Seoul Real Estate—and Taxes <<> Beneath the heated debate over Seoul's real estate market lies a fundamental question that cannot be reduced to tax policy alone. Among the Seoul of residence, the Seoul of opportunity, and the Seoul of desire—which should take priority, and which should yield? This is decided not by tax theory but by politics and legislation. What the government must do now is clear. As the Lee Jae-myung administration has emphasized, it must widen the door into Seoul and carefully manage policy so that it does not itself create new instability until supply actually arrives. The real estate market is not like the stock market, where the government can set targets, push institutional reforms, and shift the front lines in the short term. In the end, the government must do everything it can, then endure the time it takes for effects to appear.
